accounting_identity: opening stock + new build + accepted retrofit - irreversible combat loss - abandonment/capture - noncombat writeoff - retirement/scrap - shipment loss - permanently immobilized isolated garrison + repaired returns + recaptured/rebuilt hulls = dated physical residual

kill_ratio_audit_rule.definition: Enemy AFV kills and Japanese AFV losses are re-adjudicated separately. A better Japanese vehicle can raise enemy losses while also lowering Japanese writeoffs; neither is inferred from the other.
kill_ratio_audit_rule.important: A tank disabled in an action is not automatically a national loss. Battlefield possession, recovery tractors, repair capacity, route security and time before withdrawal determine whether it returns.
branch_effects: higher dispatchability creates more contacts and therefore can increase both kills and exposure
better reliability reduces noncombat attrition and abandonment
better repair/recovery converts some historical 'losses' into temporary mission-kills
better operational performance can change battlefield possession and therefore salvage rights
later Allied 75mm medium tanks can sharply increase irreversible loss despite better Japanese reliability

first_pass_findings: The current 1943-12-31 checkpoint is not a national armor inventory checkpoint.
Bengal vehicle numbers are operational motor-pool figures, not Japanese national tank stock.
Five-Go is the largest current hole for 1943 Japanese tank residual strength.
Branch-only Pacific garrisons are the largest likely hidden allocation hole.
Nomonhan is the key prewar repair-vs-writeoff audit because primary Japanese battle reports with weapon-loss appendices exist.
